File:Alpkarakush TD.png.ImageDescription: Alpkarakush is a large theropod dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic of what is now Kyrgyzstan. It is named after a large mythical bird of Kyrgyz folklore. A bipedal carnivore, Alpkarakush grew to about 8 m in body length and had a pronounced decorative structure above the brow of each eye. The initial discovery of Alpkarakush revealed a subadult and a smaller juvenile in the same locality, suggesting a degree of gregarious behavior between individuals.

File:Megalosaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Megalosaurus was the first genus of non-avian dinosaur to be validly named. A Middle Jurassic megalosaur, this species played a pivotal role in scientific understanding of prehistoric life. The creature stood at 6 m in length and weighed around 1 t. A notable theropod in its own right, the original specimen, along with Iguanodon and Hylaeosaurus defined what is considered a “dinosaur” to this day.

True to its basal dinosaur ancestry, it was a small bipedal carnivore, likely utilizing its cursorial adaptations to hunt smaller prey. Anteavis was lightly built and grew to just over 1 m in total body length, and weighed an estimated 9 kg.

File:Appalachiosaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Appalachiosaurus is one of the few tyrannosauroid dinosaurs known from eastern North America. It is known only from an estimated 6.5 m long individual, but as a juvenile, it is likely that it could grow much larger. Like all tyrannosaurs, Appalachiosaurus was a bipedal carnivore. Its arms, which would give some insight to its lifestyle, remain unknown.

The bones on display in this exhibit come from the most complete Appalachiosaurus ever discovered and represent the most complete tyrannosaur ever found in the eastern half of the United States. File:Albertosaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Albertosaurus is a large tyrannosaurid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of what is now Canada. Albertosaurus grew to about 9 m in length, and up to approximately 3 t in total body mass.

File:Asiatyrannus TD.png.ImageDescription: Asiatyrannus is a small tyrannosaur from the Late Cretaceous of what is now China. Its discovery revealed an example of niche partitioning, as it lived alongside Qianzhousaurus, a larger Asian tyrannosaur. The smaller size and more robust skull of Asiatyrannus indicate that it filled a niche often hypothesized to have been occupied by younger tyrannosaurs in the Late Cretaceous. Like all tyrannosaurs, Asiatyrannus was a carnivorous biped, and it grew to about 4 m in body length.

File:Australovenator TD.png.ImageDescription: Australovenator is the most complete predatory dinosaur discovered in Australia. It was a relatively lightweight megaraptoran theropod, measuring 6 m in length, with a body mass of 500 kg. Australovenator's arms were capable of flexing and extending far beyond any other theropod's range, giving it the ability to grasp prey toward its chest. The slender shape of the skull and relatively weak jaws also suggest that Australovenator primarily used its arms and hands while hunting.

File:The gifts of the fateful sea.jpg.ImageDescription: During the Toarcian period, the young Tethys bathed the beaches of what is now Morocco. This tropical ocean was often very violent, with recurring storms that especially hit the paradisiacal western beaches. The effects of hurricane winds bend the trunks of the trees creating surprising landscapes. They often bring back corpses of the unfortunate inhabitants of the waters, which attracts hungry Gondwanan hunters.

File:Bonapartenykus TD.png.ImageDescription: Bonapartenykus is a relatively basal alvarezsauroid dinosaur that lived approximately 71 million years ago in the Late Cretaceous of what is now Argentina. True alvarezsaurs are some of the smallest non-avian dinosaurs, but Bonapartenykus is considerably larger at about 2.5 m in length, and weighing around 70 kg. Though lacking in the fossil record, it is thought that it had the diminshed arms and single large claw that derived alvarezsaurs are known for.

File:Caletodraco TD.png.ImageDescription: Caletodraco is an abelisaurid theropod dinosaur from Late Cretaceous of what is now France. It was a fairly large bipedal carnivore at around 6 m in length. Abelisaurs are known for having shortened snouts with small teeth, and very small arms. Abelisaurs are mainly known from the southern hemisphere, especially South America. The discovery of Caletodraco in Europe reveals that their dispersal may have been more universal than previously thought.

File:Duonychus TD.png.ImageDescription: Duonychus preserved the largest keratin hand claw sheaths of any known dinosaur, at 30 cm in length. Large claws are typical for therizinosaurs, but Duonychus only had two fingers per hand, unique among the known therizinosauria. It was herbivorous, likely using these claws to pull branches toward its mouth. Duonychus was about 3 m long in total body length.

File:Dzharacursor TD.png.ImageDescription: Dzharacursor is an ornithomimid theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of what is now Uzbekistan. Ornithomimids like Dzharacursor are known for their long legs lending to a cursorial, or running, lifestyle. They had a feathered covering, and were likely omnivorous, or possibly herbivorous. Adult Dzharacursor could grow to approximately 3.5 m in length.

File:Eoabelisaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Eoabelisaurus exhibits intermittent traits between derived abelisaurs and their basal theropod ancestors. It was a bipedal carnivore reaching 6 m in length, with diminished arms, a typical abelisaur trait. The skull may have resembled more basal ceratosaurs, but due to the fragmentary nature of fossil remains, placement within ceratosauria remains unclear.

File:Jaculinykus TD.png.ImageDescription: Jaculinykus is a small alvarezsaurid theropod from the Late Cretaceous of what is now Mongolia. The name is a reference to the Jaculus, a small dragon in Greek mythology. Like other Alvarezsaurids, Jaculinykus had long legs, and enlarged first digit claws on each hand, which were probably used for digging and tearing. It also had a long tube-shaped snout filled with tiny teeth. These adaptations indicate that it probably had an insectivorous diet, feeding on colonial insects such as termites.

File:Kank TD.png.ImageDescription: Kank is an unenlagiid theropod dinosaur that grew to around 2 meters in total body length. Like all unenlagiids, it was feathered, long-legged, with a longer snout than its close dromaeosaur relatives. Its discovery bridges the geographic gap of unenlagiid dinosaurs between South America and Antarctica.

File:Kiyacursor TD.png.ImageDescription: Kiyacursor is a basal noasaurid dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of what is now Russia. Noasauridae is a diverse group of theropods closely related to abelisauridae. Though noasaurids don't superficially resemble abelisaurids to any notable degree, they are known for having a wide range of unique adaptations. Kiyacursor is estimated to have had a body length of about 2.5 m, with leg proportions suggesting that it was likely capable of running at high speeds.

File:Megapnosaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Megapnosaurus is a coelophysid theropod dinosaur from the Early Jurassic Period of Africa. It was a lightly built bipedal carnivore that grew to just over 2 m long and 13 kg in body mass. Its close relation to Coelophysis has caused some confusion in classifying the genus - it had a slender build and curved S-shaped neck, but was more robust. Comparisons between the scleral rings of Megapnosaurus and modern birds and reptiles indicate that it may have been nocturnal.

File:Meraxes TD.png.ImageDescription: Meraxes is a carcharodontosaurid theropod from the Late Cretaceous of Argentine Patagonia. It is named after a dragon from the Song of Ice and Fire fiction series by George R.R. Martin. Meraxes was a very large theropod, at about 10 m in length, and weighing approximately 4.5 t. Analysis of the holotype specimen suggests it could have been up to 53 years old when it died, having reached skeletal maturity 4 years prior to its death, making it the longest-lived non-avian theropod currently known.

File:Protathlitis TD.png.ImageDescription: Protathlitis is a genus of spinosaurid dinosaur from Spain, and the most basal member of the Baryonychinae yet discovered. Like other baryonychines, Protathlitis had curved teeth with fine serrations. It was specialized for feeding in aquatic habitats, and could grow to a length of 10-12 meters. Its discovery helped to show that the Iberian Peninsula held a diverse assemblage of spinosaurids during the Early Cretaceous, and that they migrated south to Africa to further diversify.

File:Shuvuuia TD.png.ImageDescription: Shuvuuia is a small, bird-like theropod in the family Alvarezsauridae. It is one of the smallest known non-avian dinosaurs, at just 1 m in length and weighing about 3.5 kg. Shuvuuia had a fragile skull, long legs for running, and short powerful arms with a large claw on each hand. Like all alvarezsaurids, it is thought that the small but robust arms were adapted for digging and tearing. This, along with the long tube-like snout suggest that Shuvuuia fed on colonial insects like termites. Shuvuui

File:Tyrannomimus TD.png.ImageDescription: Tyrannomimus is a basal deinocheirid whose name references a pelvic bone bearing similarity to that of tyrannosauroids. It is likely that Tyrannomimus was an omnivore, supplementing its otherwise herbivorous diet with small animal prey.

File:Vitosaura TD.png.ImageDescription: Vitosaura is an abelisaurid theropod dinosaur that lived in what is now Argentina. It was a medium sized bipedal carnivore reaching around 6 m in total body length. Though only known from the pelvic girdle, Vitosaura likely had a blunt rugose snout, and extremely short arms, as these are typical traits of abelisaurs.

File:Yuanmouraptor TD.png.ImageDescription: Yuanmouraptor is a medium-sized carnosaurian dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic of what is now China. It is a member of the metricanthosauridae, a group of theropods that is closely related to the allosaurs. As such, it has a small crest above each eye, and three fingers on each hand. Yuanmouraptor was about 5 m long in total body length.

File:Yutyrannus TD.png.ImageDescription: Yutyrannus is the largest dinosaur discovered with direct evidence of feathers. It is a large basal tyrannosauroid, growing to about 9 m in length, and weighing around 1.5 t. Yutyrannus is known from three nearly complete individuals: an adult, subadult, and a juvenile. Because they were found together, it is theorized that they may have hunted in packs. Adults sported a high midline crest on the snout, as well as one above each eye. Unlike more derived tyrannosaurs, Yutyrannus had long forearms
